# Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability

- **Authors**: Ashim Dhor, Pin-Yu Chen
- **Venue**: cs.LG
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10172>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.10172v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.57

## In one line

Treats a transformer forward pass as a controlled dynamical system with depth as time, lifts it with the Koopman operator to get a finite linear realisation whose spectrum is coordinate-free, proves that spectrum is recoverable from finite calibration data at the parametric rate, and then proves that the identifiable object and the human-legible object cannot be the same object.

## Problem

Mechanistic interpretability explains models by finding circuits in them, but has no way to say whether a circuit is a property of the model or an artifact of the procedure that found it. The evidence that this is not merely philosophical comes from sparse autoencoders: different training seeds and dictionary widths recover materially different features from the same activations, dictionaries absorb and split features, and residual-stream components remain uncaptured by any known variant. What is missing across every paradigm -- sparse dictionaries, transcoders, causal-intervention localisation, distributed alignment search -- is a theorem asserting that the discovered structure is an invariant of the model rather than of the method.

## Contributions

- A formalisation under which identifiability is a well-posed question for mechanistic interpretability: the forward pass as a depth-indexed controlled dynamical system, lifted by the Koopman operator to a finite linear realisation whose spectrum is invariant under any change of dictionary basis.
- An identifiability theorem -- stated as the first for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive -- recovering that spectrum from M calibration samples at rate M^(-1/2) up to permutation, with a matching minimax lower bound and a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations.
- A dissociation theorem: when the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and those carrying information across depth cannot coincide, since alignment would require perfect eigenvector conditioning, and measured conditioning of 10 to 100 makes the divergence unavoidable.
- The consequence that sparse-autoencoder non-identifiability is structural rather than a training artifact, with an explicit invariance penalty as remedy, shown to reduce split-half spectral distance by 41 percent at matched sparsity while degrading reconstruction, live-feature fraction and cross-seed agreement.
- An empirical section that reports its two pre-registered failures alongside its confirmations, including a criterion met in 49 percent of cells against a registered 80 percent and a universality criterion that separates seed replicas of one architecture.

## Method

The reframing is the contribution. Write the residual stream at a fixed token position as a state, the attention writes contributed by other positions as exogenous control inputs, and the MLP as autonomous nonlinear dynamics; the forward pass is then a discrete-time controlled dynamical system with depth playing the role of time. The Koopman operator, which evolves observables by composition with the dynamics, is linear in the observables even though the dynamics are nonlinear in the state, so if a dictionary of observables spans an invariant subspace the operator restricts to a finite matrix. Its eigenpairs are the Koopman modes and its eigenvalues are properties of the operator: unique up to permutation, invariant under any change of dictionary basis, and -- the main theorem -- recoverable from M calibration samples at rate M^(-1/2), with a matching minimax lower bound and a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations. A dissociation theorem then shows that whenever the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide, because alignment would require perfect eigenvector conditioning. Four practical corollaries follow: sparse-autoencoder non-identifiability is structural rather than algorithmic with an explicit invariance penalty as remedy, cross-model universality becomes a testable spectral criterion, the intervention calculus is algebraically complete on the spectral-projector algebra to first order, and balanced truncation admits an instance-dependent error certificate sharper than the classical bound in the low-effective-rank regime attention occupies. Empirically the theory is tested on GPT-2 small, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-8B-Base at 10^5 to 10^6 calibration samples, with split-half spectral distance as the convergence statistic, sequence-level block bootstraps for error bars, and pre-registered criteria for two of the corollaries.

## Results

The spectrum converges on all three models but attains the predicted -1/2 exponent on only the largest: -0.506 +/- 0.031 for Qwen3-8B-Base against -0.329 for Gemma-2-2B and -0.286 for GPT-2 small. The shortfall is explained rather than excused -- plotting each of 30 model-dictionary-width cells against its own sample threshold rather than against raw M collapses most of the scatter onto one curve, with binned medians falling from -0.31 to -0.53 and crossing -1/2 past the threshold (Spearman rho = -0.28, p < 1e-4), though the two Qwen series are named as the residual the collapse does not account for. The behavioural test is where the theory's own dissociation bites, and the authors state the negative result plainly. Ablating the top-j Koopman modes on indirect-object identification moves the logit difference more than j random directions but less than j principal directions -- at j=8, PCA removes 60 percent against the modes' 25 -- with the gap decaying 4.1-fold in depth-distance, monotonically at every layer, and essentially gone by a depth-distance of about 8. Their reading is explicitly narrow: the advantage decays to parity and does not reverse, so PCA stops being the better transport basis without the modes being shown to be one, and two causal tests of a reversal do not discriminate on this testbed because twelve layers is not enough depth to separate depth-distance from layer under a behavioural readout. No head class reaches the alignment target and greedy selection exhausts its budget at 96 of 128 modes at roughly twice the random-subspace null. The sparse-autoencoder corollary is confirmed in ordering and qualified in scope: the relative invariance residual puts SAEs furthest from Koopman invariance on every model, further even than a random orthonormal control, at 2.1x, 3.1x and 3.4x the spectral residual with the gap strengthening with scale across three SAE families -- but the ordering is conditional on the feature-selection rule, and reverses under variance-based selection (0.70x rather than 2.05x). The authors therefore restate the claim as being about the subset a practitioner is most likely to read, the features that fire often, rather than about the SAE's span. The causal test of the remedy works: raising the invariance penalty from 0 to 1 cuts the invariance residual 24 percent (0.438 to 0.333) and the split-half spectral distance -- identifiability itself rather than a proxy -- by 41 percent (0.0170 to 0.0101) at matched sparsity, while reconstruction degrades (fraction of variance unexplained 0.222 to 0.255), the live-feature fraction falls from 0.77 to 0.58, cross-seed feature agreement moves the wrong way, and at a penalty of 10 the dictionary collapses outright across all three seeds. Two pre-registered results fail their controls and are reported as failures: the SAE-gap criterion is met in 49 percent of 75 cells against a registered 80 percent, because the sign of the effect tracks the feature-selection rule; and the universality criterion separates two seed replicas of one architecture, so in its stated form it is not a universality criterion.

## Limitations

Stated at length and ordered by how much they constrain the claims. The estimand depends on modelling conventions the authors cannot fully justify -- residualising the attention write against the lifted state moves the spectrum by 6.8 to 9.1 times the resolution floor, so the naive and residualised conventions specify different estimands at the achievable precision, and both are reported. Invariance holds only approximately: every theorem assumes the dictionary spans an invariant subspace, real dictionaries satisfy this approximately, and the resulting bias does not vanish as M grows, so the method is not model-agnostic and the dictionary must be co-designed with the architecture -- though within a fixed dictionary family it is uniform across corpus, seed and hyperparameter, which is precisely the property SAEs lack. Diagonalisability and spectral separation are generic but not universal, and exact coincidence is conjectured measure-zero but not proved. The intervention calculus is proved to first order but never validated against measured patching effects. The rate is asymptotic in a way that bites, since the constant is unknown and the sample threshold is an order-of-magnitude guide. The random-Fourier dictionary bandwidth, fixed rather than retuned per model, degrades at width 4096 in the deepest layers, which the authors identify as a dictionary-construction failure rather than a model or estimator failure. And two stated results fail their pre-registered controls, reported because both bound what may be claimed. Not stated but worth noticing: three models and one behavioural task carry the entire empirical section, and the strongest theoretical claim -- that the identifiable and the legible object cannot coincide -- is supported empirically by one circuit on one testbed the authors themselves say is too shallow to separate the relevant variables.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: This is the paper the archive's accumulated worry about sparse autoencoders has been pointing at: it asks whether a discovered structure is a property of the model or of the finder, and answers it for one primitive with a theorem rather than an argument. Two results matter regardless of whether Koopman spectral analysis is adopted. First, it makes SAE run-to-run variability structural rather than a training defect -- the reconstruction-and-sparsity objective does not enforce the invariance that identifiability requires -- and then does the thing that turns a diagnosis into evidence: adds the missing term and shows the outcome moves, cutting split-half spectral distance 41 percent at matched sparsity. It also reports the price honestly, with reconstruction degrading, live features falling from 0.77 to 0.58, cross-seed agreement moving the wrong way, and the dictionary collapsing at a higher penalty, leaving open whether a dictionary can be sparse, reconstructive and invariant at once. Second, and more consequential for how the archive reads interpretability claims generally, the dissociation theorem says that in the non-normal regime these models occupy, the directions carrying variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide -- so the identifiable object and the legible object are different objects, and a safety case needing both needs two tools and must say which it is using where. That is a formal version of a boundary the archive keeps hitting empirically, and it sits alongside detection-versus-control as a second reason a single decomposition cannot serve every purpose. The paper is also a model of reporting that the archive should hold up as a standard. It states plainly that the modes lose to PCA on the one behavioural task (25 percent against 60 at j=8), that the advantage decays to parity without reversing, that its causal tests of a reversal do not discriminate on a twelve-layer testbed, that its headline SAE ordering inverts under a different feature-selection rule, and that two pre-registered criteria fail -- one met in 49 percent of cells against a registered 80, and a universality criterion that separates seed replicas of one architecture and therefore is not one. Cite the theory as theory: three models and one circuit carry the empirical section, and the intervention calculus is proved but never checked against measured patching effects.

## Abstract

Mechanistic interpretability explains models by identifying circuits inside them, but has no way to tell whether a circuit is a property of the model or an artifact of the method that found it. Sparse autoencoders illustrate the problem: different seeds and widths recover materially different features from the same activations, and no theory says whether that variability is incidental or structural. We put dictionary learning for interpretability on an identifiability footing. Treating the forward pass as a controlled dynamical system with depth as time and lifting it with the Koopman operator yields a finite linear realisation whose \emph{spectrum} is a coordinate-free property of the model. We prove the spectrum is recoverable from $M$ calibration samples at rate $M^{-1/2}$ up to permutation - to our knowledge the first identifiability theorem for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive, with a matching minimax lower bound, a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations, and a dissociation theorem: whenever the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide. The identifiable object and the legible object are not the same object. On GPT-2 small, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-8B-Base the spectrum converges everywhere and attains the predicted exponent on Qwen3-8B-Base ($0.506 \pm 0.031$); shortfalls collapse onto one curve against each cell's sample threshold. Koopman modes beat random directions but lose to principal components on indirect-object identification, with the gap decaying $4.1\times$ in depth-distance, as the theorem predicts. The Koopman spectrum is an identifiable, model-intrinsic fingerprint with a stated error bar, not a legible decomposition.
